exchanges.question: No analyst question: exchange 1 holds the company's scripted remarks and quarter discussion on results, tariffs, regional markets, construction, inventory, guidance and precision ag innovation.
exchanges.answer: Net sales and revenues up 5% to $13.369 billion; equipment operations net sales up 5% to $11.778 billion with 16.9% margin, helped by a $272 million IEEPA tariff refund that lifted margins by nearly 2.5 points; net income $1.773 billion or $6.55 per diluted share. FY2026 net income guide held at $4.5 billion-$5 billion, direct tariff exposure about $1.2 billion (about $900 million net of refunds), South America industry cut to down 15% from down 5%, C&F net sales raised to up about 20%. Baseline view is that 2026 is the bottom of the ag cycle, and $635 million was returned to shareholders in the quarter.

exchanges.question: With the construction industry forecast at up 5% versus Deere's much stronger sales growth, is the industry healthy and is Deere gaining a lot of share?
exchanges.answer: Beal: last year's front-loaded earthmoving underproduction gives a natural lift as production aligns with retail this year; the industry guide is up 5% in earthmoving with continued strength in road building; and Deere has seen some share pickup over the past 12 months, particularly the last six or so after pricing adjustments at the end of last year. No share figure given.

exchanges.question: What is the baseline margin in each business, and how does the $272 million tariff refund break down between segments?
exchanges.answer: Beal: tariff expense run rate unchanged at about $1.2 billion for the full year, split about 45% C&F, about a third Small Ag & Turf and about 20% large ag, a full-year impact of about 3 points. The $272 million refund is about a point of tailwind for equipment operations on a full-year basis, split about 50% C&F, 30% Small Ag & Turf and 20% large ag. Baseline segment margins were not given.

exchanges.question: What tariff mitigation strategies has Deere pursued over the last 12 months with no pricing taken, and what more could come?
exchanges.answer: Norwood: equipment operations price forecast is about 1.5% to 2%, matching general inflation ex-tariffs of also about 1.5%-2%, so tariff costs are somewhat margin dilutive; no surcharges, and mitigation is via cost actions (resourcing, reshoring, exemption submissions, USMCA compliance) which he expects to largely counter tariffs over the coming periods. Beal: price and production cost comparisons get more favorable in the back half of 2026 as Deere laps last year's incentives, tariff expense and inflation, so price-cost improves.

exchanges.question: How should downside risk to regional outlooks be framed given the geopolitical environment, and are there historical periods to reference for farmer behavior?
exchanges.answer: Beal: a couple of years into the downturn, fleet ages are very elevated for high horsepower tractors and combines, and used inventory has healthed (model year 2022 and 2023 high horsepower tractors down about 45% from peak a year ago); customer margins are pressured by fertilizer, and Brazil also faces currency headwinds. Baseline expectation remains recovery in 2027 with some replacement returning, pace dependent on policy, ag fundamentals and geopolitics. Seibert: U.S. soybean and corn prices up about 20% since August with inputs secured ahead of planting, while Brazil sees input costs earlier. No historical analog was given.

exchanges.question: What are the order trends in large ag seasonal products and any regional trends standing out?
exchanges.answer: Beal: 2026 production plans are set because the early order programs have closed for combines, sprayers and planters. The MY2027 sprayer EOP opened at the beginning of May and runs through the end of August; planters open at the beginning of June and run through the end of September. Very early, but what has been seen supports the view that 2026 still marks the bottom of the ag cycle. No regional detail or order figures given.

exchanges.question: What is expected See & Spray acreage this year, how are retrofit orders tracking, what are Precision Essentials renewal rates for the 2025 cohort, and are list prices rising on advanced EOP features?
exchanges.answer: Beal: See & Spray covered 1 million acres in year one and 5 million acres globally last year; the same customers are spraying more acres year to date, with 50%-60% herbicide savings demonstrated over two years; See & Spray Green on Green was introduced in Brazil and 2027 take rates so far exceed this year's. Precision Essentials renewals are in the 70% range overall and over 90% for the second-year cohort; Seibert: more than 4,000, closer to 5,000, new customer orgs in Operations Center. Harvest automation utilization over 60% in Northern Hemisphere and over 80% in Brazil. No 2026 acre target, retrofit or list price answer given.

exchanges.question: What is the cadence for 3Q and 4Q on sales and margins, and what by region or segment could cause the second half to deviate from normal seasonality?
exchanges.answer: Beal: back half higher than front half, Q4 a little higher than Q3. Large ag has Q4 a bit stronger than Q3 with more Waterloo large tractor shipments to North America in the back half than the front, which is abnormal; Small Ag & Turf follows normal seasonality with a step down in Q3 and another in Q4; C&F is fairly balanced with Q4 maybe slightly stronger.

exchanges.question: Are large ag pricing expectations more conservative than peers, and does that reflect higher discounting?
exchanges.answer: Beal: price was adjusted down this quarter because of Brazil; all regions are expected to be price positive in large ag, with a 1% full-year price guide, North America a bit better and the other two a little lower. Seibert: second-half price will look a little better than the first half given earlier discounting and used-inventory progress. Peer comparison and discounting level not directly addressed.

exchanges.question: Is the $270 million IEEPA refund a true benefit versus the initial guide, or offset by other tariffs back to $1.2 billion? How can price-cost improve through the year when raw materials, components and energy costs point to tougher conditions?
exchanges.answer: Beal: the $1.2 billion tariff expense run rate is unchanged from last quarter and the $272 million refund is new, so net is about $900 million this year; material inflation came in over the quarter, but the back half laps last year's tariffs and indirect inflation, so comps get more favorable, and he agrees there is high inflation over the last two or three months. Norwood: pricing is much more favorable in the back half, price-cost ratios improve meaningfully, and large ag factories get better Q4 absorption with significantly higher production rates.

exchanges.question: What sentiment and feedback are Deere and its North American dealers hearing on large ag and the spring early order program, as a first read on 2027 capex?
exchanges.answer: Beal: baseline is some level of recovery next year on fleet age and inventory actions; John Deere Financial trade wholesale (used equipment financed on dealer lots) is down over 15%; about a third of the old crop still needs to be sold, and there is a bit more caution on input costs. Norwood: dealer feedback varies, with dealers who took early action on used most optimistic and a couple looking to add to used fleets, others more moderate. No EOP forecast given.

exchanges.question: Is share gain in South America coming from the existing portfolio or from new products?
exchanges.answer: Beal: share has risen steadily and fairly linearly over the last decade and a half in tractors and combines, supported by new products and technologies, the dealer channel and localization; this year topped last year's record introduction with new combines, sprayers, planters, See & Spray and Starlink connectivity. Harvest settings automation for combines has the highest utilization globally in Brazil, and Deere is extremely bullish on the region. No split between existing and new products given.
